Each prompt starts with a <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change. Follow the block at the top of the prompt you are answering; an earlier prompt's block no longer applies.

Its code is located in ./src.

Its spec's Piton source, in ./spec, is only where edits to the spec go.

Read the spec from its compiled reference under .claude/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

Never read the .pi source under ./spec to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to .claude/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.
instructions:
We're only asking a question about the project. Answer it without changing anything.

When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read .suspense/suspense-fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

The code is located in ./src.

The spec's Piton source is in ./spec, which `piton slice` reads. Don't change it, and don't read it directly to learn what the spec says: read the compiled reference, or what `piton slice` prints, instead.

Whenever the user asks you for a prompt, or your answer suggests one for them to send, give each prompt as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, one of `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text, ready to send, never as plain text, a quote, or any other code block, since only this form lets the user send it from your answer. Pick the mode that fits the work, `chain` when it changes both the spec and the code; the user can send it to Code, Chain, or Spec all the same. When you need the user to answer something before you can go on, write the question as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, the question on its first lines and then, if there are answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Use these blocks only for prompts and questions meant for the user, never for code or examples.

#### Diagnostics

Suspense keeps a log of what updating does, `updates.log` in its own data directory, beside its preferences, as the [UserPreferencesScope](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope) keeps them: one line per step, with the time, each check with the repository and running version it checked for, the releases it found and the one it took or why it took none, each download with its asset, size, and digest check, each staging, each putting in place with its paths and how it went, and each launch's confirmation, every failure with its whole error. It keeps the last 1,000 lines.
The Updates section has a "Details" disclosure, collapsed to start with, that shows what updating rests on: the running version, the repository it updates from, or that it has none and so is not an edge build, the running binary's path and whether its directory can be written, the last check's time and the newest release it found, and what is staged, if anything, with a "Show log" button that opens `updates.log` as the [OpenFileScope](../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) opens a file, and a "Copy" button that puts all of it, with the log's last 50 lines, on the clipboard, for a bug report.

content.text:
That's a good idea, and the spec already has a model for it. SelfUpdateScope › Diagnostics keeps `updates.log` in Suspense's data directory: one timestamped line per step, every failure with its whole error, capped at 1,000 lines, with "Show log" and "Copy" buttons. Nothing like that exists for the rest of the app.

What there is today:
- **Task and question history records.** They keep the harness's output, but without timing for each step.
- **`eprintln!` calls.** They're scattered across about ten modules. In a Windows release build they go nowhere, because there's no console.
- **No panic log.** A crash leaves no trace.

**What I'd log**
- **Every child process:** the command, its working folder, how long it took, its exit status, and its stderr when it fails. Child processes all go through `crate::process::command` now, so this can be added in one place.
- **Each task's phases, with timestamps:** queued, spec build, snapshot, preparing the container, harness started, first event, each tool call, result, and the after-snapshot. This would answer "why is my prompt slow" with numbers instead of guesses. The same timings belong in the task's history record.
- **Container runs:** the mounts and the full `podman` command line.
- **Background work:** git status refreshes, spec builds and LSP restarts, with how long each took, and a warning when the UI thread stalls.
- **Panics:** with a backtrace, written before the app dies.
- **Not logged:** environment variables or tokens. Prompt text belongs in the history, not the log.

To hand it to an agent, add a command that writes a single folder: the recent log, `updates.log`, the app's version and platform, the harness report, and the history records of the last few tasks. You'd point the debugging agent at that folder.

```suspense-prompt chain
Suspense keeps a debug log of what it does, so that a problem can be handed to an agent as files to investigate. It is `suspense.log` in Suspense's own data directory, beside `updates.log`, as the SelfUpdateScope keeps that one, one line per event, each with the time to the millisecond, the project it concerns, and what happened, keeping the last 20,000 lines across sessions.

It logs every child process the application starts, its command, working directory, how long it took, and its exit status, with its standard error when it failed; each task's and question's phases as they happen, queued, spec build, snapshot, preparing the container with its mounts and the podman command, harness started, its first event, each tool call, its result, and the closing snapshot, each with how long it took; each git status refresh, spec build, and language server start or restart, with how long it took; any time the window was unresponsive for more than 200 milliseconds; and every panic, with its backtrace, written before the application exits. It never logs environment variables, credentials, or prompt text. A task's history record also keeps the times of its phases.

The command palette has a "Collect debug info" command that writes a folder, named for the time, in Suspense's data directory and shows it in the file manager: the debug log, `updates.log`, the application's version, platform, and harness report, and the history records of the open project's last ten tasks and questions, with a short README saying what each file is. The palette also has "Open debug log", which opens `suspense.log` as the OpenFileScope opens a file.
```
